allegations.text: In a two-phase sanctions proceeding, the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon struck plaintiff's summary-judgment briefs, dismissed claims with prejudice, and imposed sanctions on pro hac vice counsel Stephen Brigandi for submitting briefing containing non-existent cases and fabricated quotations that the court attributed to an unidentified AI tool. A December 2025 order imposed a $15,500 Rule 11 sanction; the March 2026 order finalized a fee award of $94,704.38 apportioned 85% to Brigandi and 15% to local counsel Timothy Murphy.

allegations.reliance_or_harm: $15,500 monetary sanction on Brigandi; $94,704.38 attorney-fee award ($80,498.72 Brigandi, $14,205.66 Murphy); claims dismissed with prejudice; summary-judgment briefs stricken.

Eaton denied using AI, but the court found his denial "incredible" because he had himself attached CoCounsel-generated documents. The order was directed published in the Federal Supplement and referred to the Alabama State Bar.

Watkins of Burrill Watkins LLC was publicly reprimanded, disqualified from the case, and sanctioned a combined $47,056.90 after forensic examination of his firm's ChatGPT Business Plan workspace confirmed hallucinated citations in filings. allegations.text: Defense counsel in a wage-and-hour class action admitted using LexisNexis's AI tool to help construct submissions without reviewing them for correctness, resulting in AI-hallucinated citations. The court imposed $1,710 in attorneys' fees (AI-authority-related) and a $1,000 monetary penalty on defense counsel under Rule 37, 28 U.S.C. § 1927, and inherent powers. A separate $46,980 discovery sanction was also imposed on defendants for unrelated witness-declaration misconduct.

The court characterized the citations as "hallucinations generated by an artificial intelligence research tool" and specifically named Fastcase. The district judge reduced the Magistrate's recommended $7,500 sanction to $2,000.

The brief was drafted by contracted attorney Farah Chalisa using ChatGPT, and filed by counsel of record Abdullah Salah. Salah was sanctioned $5,000 under Fed. R. App. P. 46(c); Chalisa was referred to the Illinois ARDC but not directly sanctioned because she had not appeared before the circuit.

Document metadata showed the filings originated from a program in the client's name. Despite the defendant denying AI use, the court made an express, unhedged finding of generative-AI misuse — the first reported GenAI sanctions decision at the New York appellate level. Sanctions of $7,500 were imposed on counsel and $2,500 on the client.

allegations.reliance_or_harm: $10,000 in sanctions ($7,500 on attorney Douglass + $2,500 on LeTennier); appeals affirmed with costs.
allegations.source_locator: Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v. LeTennier, 2026 NY Slip Op 00040, Docket No. CV-23-0713 (N.Y. App. Div., 3d Dep’t)

At the show-cause hearing he acknowledged using AI tools available through Westlaw, and his written response admitted his firm has the "Precision" version of Westlaw, which the court described as "a generative AI tool offered by Westlaw." Mitchell attributed the text to an unidentifiable prior template whose origin he could not recall, and admitted he had verified none of the citations. He then filed an untimely proposed reply brief purporting to withdraw eight cases, none of which matched the original eight, and all eight substitutes were also hallucinated. The court made its own finding of AI use in the published opinion, stating that counsel had outsourced his legal work to an AI algorithm; no product is named and counsel made no admission, conceding only that his citations were erroneous or unverifiable. The conduct continued after a warning.

R., Addendum 8, r. 2(C).
allegations.source_locator: Akerlund v. Atlas Air, Inc., Flight Services International, LLC, No. 24-11033 (11th Cir.)

allegations.text: An assistant district attorney used artificial-intelligence software to draft the State’s briefs opposing a motion for new trial, a proposed order for the trial court, and the State’s appellate brief, without independently verifying the citations it produced. The trial court signed the proposed order largely as submitted, so the fabricated authority entered a judge’s signed ruling. The Supreme Court of Georgia identified at least nine defective citations in that order, twelve further cases the prosecutor herself later identified in her trial-court briefing, and nine authorities withdrawn from the State’s appellate brief.

allegations.deployer: Assistant District Attorney Deborah L. Leslie, Clayton County District Attorney’s Office

allegations.mitigation_gap: The prosecutor did not verify AI-generated citations before filing, and the reviewing court signed a proposed order without independent checking — two verification failures compounding, with the second laundering the first into a judicial act.
allegations.reliance_or_harm: Prosecutor and the Clayton County district attorney’s office admonished; the prosecutor’s privilege to practise before the Supreme Court of Georgia suspended for six months, reinstatement conditioned on 12 hours of continuing legal education beyond normal requirements covering ethics, brief writing, and the proper use of artificial-intelligence software; the trial court’s order denying a new trial vacated and the case remanded for a new order free of fabricated citations.

Defence counsel admitted relying on a separate in-house AI research tool, which the order expressly calls “this unnamed software”, also without verification. One of the protester’s attorneys confirmed he had used Westlaw’s AI tool CoCounsel in preparing the supplemental protest, the attorneys acknowledged some of its citations were erroneous, and the attorney admittedly failed to correct all of them before filing.

The court found Rule 11 violations by Watson and reviewing signatory Nick Norris, held Watson & Norris, PLLC jointly responsible, and sanctioned supervisory attorney Louis H. Watson Jr. after finding that the firm failed to contain a broader pattern of tainted filings despite prior notice and an internal policy restricting external AI use.

allegations.text: Attorney Mason Cole filed appellate briefs on behalf of a workplace-discrimination petitioner containing nonexistent case citations and fabricated statutory language. In response to the court's show-cause order he stated that he uses a premier corporate subscription of ChatGPT to synthesize complex matters, including this case, and that he had cross-referenced citations with LexisNexis but overlooked that several did not exist or did not support the propositions cited. The court identified ten distinct false citations or misstatements of law.
allegations.asserted_by: asserting party not identified in the indexed source fields
allegations.deployer: Mason Cole, of Cole Sadkin, LLC, counsel for petitioner Kimberly Scott
allegations.canonical_source_conflicted: Nonexistent Illinois appellate authority, fabricated statutory language including a supposed 'full investigation' requirement under the Illinois Human Rights Act, and counsel's duties under Illinois Supreme Court Rules 341(h)(5) and 375(b)
allegations.mitigation_gap: Counsel relied on ChatGPT output for appellate research and represented that he cross-checked citations against LexisNexis, but that verification did not catch citations that were nonexistent or that failed to support the cited proposition; he attributed the failure to inexperience in appellate practice.
allegations.reliance_or_harm: The court affirmed the underlying dismissal, fined counsel $15,000 payable to the clerk of the Appellate Court within 30 days at a rate of $1,500 per false citation or misstatement, and directed the clerk to send a copy of the opinion to the Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission. The court recorded that the misconduct forced it to verify the fabricated citations, research nationwide sanctions law, and order and review counsel's response.
allegations.source_locator: Scott v. Illinois Human Rights Commission, 2026 IL App (1st) 251462, No. 1-25-1462

allegations.text: Defense counsel Hilary Miller filed a motion to dismiss and a motion to exclude extrinsic evidence containing fabricated citations and fabricated quotations from real cases. At the show-cause hearing he stated that this was the first and only matter in which he used artificial intelligence, that he used a paid tool called Open Law for argument and case suggestions, and that he also used Claude and ChatGPT for additional suggestions. He Shepardized every case through Lexis but did not verify that pin cites referred to the correct page or that quotations were accurate.
allegations.asserted_by: asserting party not identified in the indexed source fields
allegations.ai_system_name: Open Law, Claude and ChatGPT (named; admitted)
allegations.deployer: Hilary Miller, defense counsel for Tacobarn Newtown LLC and Tacobarn Greenwich LLC
allegations.canonical_source_conflicted: Fabricated quotations attributed to Ashcroft v. Iqbal and other real decisions, together with nonexistent supporting authority, against counsel's certification duties under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(2)
allegations.mitigation_gap: Counsel's verification step confirmed that the cited cases existed and remained good law but did not check whether the quoted language or pin cites were real, which is precisely the failure mode generative AI produces; the court found the inadequate inquiry weighed in favour of sanctions.
allegations.reliance_or_harm: The court imposed a $3,500 monetary sanction and referred the matter to the Grievance Committee under its local rules. The court set out a three-category definition of AI hallucination in legal research and warned that hallucinated or severely misstated law will often result in sanctions regardless of whether AI tools were used.
allegations.source_locator: Barteca Holdings LLC v. Tacobarn Newtown LLC, No. 3:26-cv-00250-VDO (D. Conn.), ECF No. 43

allegations.text: Between November and December 2025 plaintiff's counsel Jocelyn Stewart filed multiple submissions containing dozens of inaccurate factual and legal citations. She later averred that she used Claude and ChatGPT to draft the submissions, that the programs generated the false citations, and that she did not review their outputs because she believed the tools operated in a closed system limited to documents she supplied. She continued to submit a hallucinated citation in December, after opposing counsel had first raised AI concerns at oral argument.
allegations.asserted_by: asserting party not identified in the indexed source fields
allegations.deployer: Jocelyn Stewart, counsel for plaintiff Joann LeDoux
allegations.canonical_source_conflicted: Dozens of nonexistent or materially altered case citations and quotations whose meaning had been changed, against counsel's certification duties under Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)
allegations.mitigation_gap: Counsel adopted a mistaken belief that a closed-system retrieval setup could not hallucinate and therefore performed no verification of AI output, despite having previously heard of an attorney sanctioned for the same conduct and despite numerous Ninth Circuit courts having issued or threatened comparable sanctions before her filings.
allegations.reliance_or_harm: The court found the conduct akin to contempt, imposed a $3,000 personal sanction on counsel payable within 21 days, and required her to provide a copy of the order to her client and certify that she had done so. Counsel had earlier been required to withdraw or amend the affected motions and ceased using AI to generate quotations or citations for filings. On 18 August 2026 the court granted Defendants' Daubert motions, excluding both of Plaintiff's remaining experts. It found that multiple hallucinated citations to academic articles in Dr. Gabriel Holguin's report irreparably undermined his credibility and that Plaintiff had not met her burden to show the opinion was based on sufficient facts or data, citing among other things the AI-generated list of materials supposedly relied upon and Dr. Holguin's lack of diligence. The court then granted summary judgment and dismissed Plaintiff's remaining claims with prejudice.
allegations.source_locator: LeDoux v. Outliers, Inc., No. 3:24-cv-05808-TMC (W.D. Wash.), ECF No. 265

allegations.text: Attorney Ian G. Gottlieb and his firm filed applications for certification to file public interest appeals under General Statutes section 52-265a in two related landlord-tenant matters. The applications contained hallucinated citations produced by generative AI used during the editing and review process, and after the Chief Justice granted the applications the briefs filed in each case also contained hallucinated citations. At a show-cause hearing counsel candidly admitted that filing approximately seven erroneous and unverified citations as a result of generative-AI use violated at a minimum rule 1.1 of the Rules of Professional Conduct.
allegations.asserted_by: asserting party not identified in the indexed source fields
allegations.deployer: Ian G. Gottlieb and GLG Law, LLC
allegations.canonical_source_conflicted: Approximately seven fabricated or inaccurately generated citations, against rule 1.1 of the Connecticut Rules of Professional Conduct and counsel's duty of candour to the court
allegations.mitigation_gap: Generative AI was introduced at the editing and review stage rather than at drafting, so the output bypassed the verification counsel had applied earlier; counsel had initially used LexisNexis for research and the defective citations entered through the later AI-assisted pass.
allegations.reliance_or_harm: The court ordered Attorney Gottlieb to complete six hours of continuing legal education in ethics and law office management beyond his annual requirement, three of which must concern generative AI, and ordered Gottlieb and the law firm each to donate $1,000 to the CT Bar Institute, Inc. Both must file a compliance report with the Appellate Clerk and send a courtesy copy to the Statewide Grievance Committee.
allegations.source_locator: TOV Realty, LLC v. Suarez (SC 21183) and Kosel Equity, LLC v. MacGregor (SC 21184), 355 Conn. 902 (2026)
